 With the golf season winding down, now's a good time to make the most of your remaining rounds and think about what could help you play better next year. If a golf watch is on your Christmas wishlist, there are plenty of options worth considering, from models that offer accurate GPS distances to those that track your shots and help you analyse your performance.
 Golf watches can also keep tabs on your daily activity, with many offering health and fitness features you'd expect from the best smartwatches . Their real value, though, comes on the course, where detailed maps, hazard distances and green layouts can help you plan each shot and make smarter decisions throughout your round.
 Of course, no watch can fix a wayward swing for you (if only). The right one can, however, give you more information to work with, helping you make better-informed decisions on the course and spot areas to work on before your next round. That's why we've tested golf watches from reputable brands including Garmin and Shot Scope to find out which features are genuinely useful when you're playing.
 Every watch in this guide has been personally tested by our experts, with scores out of five for design, features, performance and value. We've used those scores alongside our hands-on experience to choose the best options for different golfers, so you can spend less time comparing specs and more time thinking about your next round.

While it might be one of the more expensive options, the display is crisp, clear, and bright.  Notably, it comes preloaded with course data from 43,000 tracks around the world, making it useful pretty much anywhere. You'll get distance accuracy, help with yardages, a hole map, and hazard information too.
 There's also shot tracking data and a companion app for recording your scores. You'll even get Garmin's Enhanced PlaysLike Distance feature that gives yardage based on topography data and even wind direction.
 You also get Garmin's great suite of health and fitness features, so you can use it off the course as well as on. There's also GPS, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and a 5ATM water rating for those wet days. A premium golf watch with a price tag to match, the S70 is king right now.

Channelling that TAG Heuer pedigree, this is a sleek, chic, robust, and well-designed golf watch. It's comfy to wear, strong and tough, has a secure fit, and is beautifully finished.

The Calibre E4 Golf Edition's golf functionality is excellent, and combined with the TAG Heuer pedigree and terrific smartwatch functionality, ensuring it offers the fullest package going.
 Specifically, there are more than 40,000 preloaded courses available, and a virtual caddie that will learn your shots and distances so it can suggest the best match in future rounds. One can critique it slightly for not offering the most bleeding-edge golf features in 2024 that some competitors can offer such as green contour depiction, and 'plays like' functionality, but those are brand-new features on the very latest watches.  If you're looking for the best value of the bunch, the Garmin Approach S50 is the winner of this guide. During testing, our reviewer Rob Dwiar found it delivered much of what makes the flagship S70 such an excellent golf watch, but at a considerably lower price. Unless you specifically want the S70's exclusive features, the S50 offers exceptional bang for your buck.
 On the course, the S50 impressed with accurate yardages, automatic shot tracking, score logging and Garmin's excellent PlaysLike Distance feature, which factors in elevation and weather to give you a more realistic distance to the pin. Rob also praised its bright AMOLED display, lightweight design and comfortable fit, making it just as easy to wear for everyday use as it is for 18 holes.
 Away from the course, you still get Garmin's excellent health and fitness tracking, including sleep monitoring, Body Battery and stress tracking, so it won't spend the rest of the week gathering dust in a drawer.

 The Shot Scope V3 was our top pick for a long time when it comes to shot tracking, and the V5 is a worthy successor.
 It continues the formula of value for money and easy of use. It might not be the most premium option – it only comes in one color and there's no touchscreen – but you also get 16 free club tags for shot tracking and analysis. These attach to the butt of your club's grip and will automatically record data from each shot, giving you helpful information to help you improve your game. Most other manufacturers charge either for the tags or a subscription to use them, so getting them for free with the V5 makes this pick a no-brainer.
 The V3 had automatic shot tracking after your hits, but you have to activate manually with the V5. That means you need to activate the track option after hitting a shot which takes some getting used to.
 Overall though, the Shot Scope V5 is excellent value for money, much cheaper than many of the other options on the market, and you get those club tags for shot analysis thrown in.

 How to choose the best golf watch for you 
 The best golf watch for you will depend on a variety of different factors. Firstly, it needs to be the right price for you, whether you’re after a high-end premium watch or a more conservatively-priced model. It needs to have the right features for you. If you struggle with club choice, you're better off with one of the premium models which has Garmin's 'virtual caddie' club recommendation functionality. If you'd rather not have this feature, you could save some money and opt for the Garmin Approach S12.
 It's also worth checking if your local courses are available pre-loaded onto the watch, or available to download on Garmin, SkyGolf or Shot Scope's companion apps. If your stomping grounds aren't available, you may not get all the functionalities you want.
 You might need more typical smartwatch features such as sleep tracking, heart rate monitoring and notification functions, or you might prefer a wristwatch with slimmed-down features to save money on the total price. SkyCaddie LX5's simple pedometer and heart rate functions don't hold a candle to Garmin's features, which crib from its wildly successful fitness and running watches.
 Finally, check the battery life. If you don't like charging your watch between games, you'll want to plump for an S62, while watches with a shorter battery life will need you to remember to charge each time you head out the door.
 Below, we’ve answered a couple of your most-asked questions, as well as an insight into how we test each watch as we get them.
 What is a golf rangefinder?
 A rangefinder is a tool that helps you measure the distance between you and your target, using either GPS or a laser. GPS rangefinders (as found in golf watches) are faster to use, but laser ones are more accurate. Golf watches and rangefinders are slightly different, but using a wrist-mounted GPS device can act in place of a free-standing laser rangefinder. 
 Does Fitbit make a golf watch?
 Fitbit doesn't make a dedicated golf watch, but all of Fitbit's GPS-enabled watches have a golf-tracking mode that you can use to monitor calories burned during your game. This will only be accurate if you're walking though, not using a golf buggy.

 We test each of the best golf watches comprehensively. We look at the watch’s tracking technology, battery life, and compatibility with different phones. Does it have the technology to track and calculate the distance of your shots? Can its GPS technology map your favorite courses?
 We take each watch for several test-drives on real golf courses to test all their key features.

 The best fitness trackers do far more than count steps. Today's wearables can help you understand how well you've slept, whether you're recovered enough to train, how your heart is performing and even when it's time to take a rest day. Better still, you don't need to spend flagship smartwatch money to benefit from those insights.
 The category has evolved dramatically over the last few years, too. Alongside familiar fitness bands, you'll now find lightweight GPS watches, discreet smart rings and even screen-free trackers that quietly collect health data without constantly demanding your attention. Choosing the right one is less about finding the device with the longest feature list and more about finding the one that fits your lifestyle.
 Our team has spent more than a decade testing fitness trackers, smartwatches and wearable technology from Garmin , Apple , Fitbit , Samsung , Amazfit and many more. We judge every device on tracking accuracy, battery life, comfort, software, training tools and overall value, wearing each one for weeks before deciding whether it deserves a place in this guide.

 How to choose the best fitness tracker 
 When choosing a fitness tracker, start by thinking about how you exercise. If you're mainly interested in tracking daily activity, sleep and general wellness (such as recovery, stress, heart health and overall activity levels), a simple fitness band or screenless tracker may be all you need. However, if you run, cycle or spend a lot of time training outdoors, it's worth looking for a device with built-in GPS so it can accurately track your routes and pace without relying on your phone.
 Next, consider how much data you actually want. Some trackers focus on simple metrics like steps, heart rate and sleep, while others provide detailed training analysis, recovery insights and personalised coaching. More information isn't always better, so think about whether you'll use those extra metrics before paying for them.
 Comfort matters too. A fitness tracker proves the most useful when you wear it consistently, so it's worth considering how it will fit into your everyday life. If you already wear a traditional watch, a smart ring such as the Samsung Galaxy Ring or a screenless tracker like the Google Fitbit Air or Amazfit Helio Strap can be a good alternative, offering health and activity tracking without adding another watch-sized device to your wrist.
 Finally, think about the display. Devices with bright AMOLED screens are generally easier to read at a glance and outdoors in bright sunlight, while simpler fitness bands often prioritise battery life over display quality. If you plan to check your stats regularly throughout the day, a larger, sharper screen may be worth the extra cost.
 What is a fitness tracker?
 A fitness tracker is a device, typically a wristband, that monitors statistics such as your heart rate, the number of steps you take each day, and how long you spend working out. You might think of Fitbit bands as the quintessential tracker, but Apple Watches and other devices, such as smart rings, are fitness trackers too. 
 Most fitness trackers have several dedicated modes for recording different forms of exercise, and some also have GPS for tracking your location during runs, walks and bike rides. Most fitness trackers also monitor how long you spend sleeping, and in each sleep stage.
 All this data is sent to an app on your smartphone, where you can track changes over time. Most apps give you virtual 'awards' for achieving particular goals, such as taking 10,000 steps per day or going to bed on time.
 Why do you need a fitness tracker?
 It can be tough to break old habits and develop new ones, and a fitness tracker can help give you the encouragement you need. Tracking the number of steps you take each day and aiming for a particular target might be simple, but it can push you to make simple changes (like getting off the bus a stop earlier, or walking short distances rather than driving), which can add up to make a significant difference over time.
 Which fitness trackers are most accurate?
 Most modern fitness trackers do an excellent job in tracking heart rate, stress and sleep accurately. Fitness trackers have optical heart rate sensors that can keep up with quick changes in heart rate. 
 Some have GPS to better track running, walking and cycling workouts outdoors. This is generally an estimation, but if you run, walk or cycle frequently and want to closely track those workouts, it's best to choose a tracker with GPS as it can monitor your routes, distance travelled, and speed. 
 Check our full reviews for more information: we test fitness trackers against each other and industry gold standards, such as the Apple Watch Ultra 3 or Polar H10 heart rate monitor , to determine whether there are significant differences in GPS and heart rate readings.
 What makes a good fitness tracker?
 A good fitness tracker is one that you'll wear every day and will help you build up a complete picture of your health. With that knowledge, you can start to make small tweaks that will help you sleep better, lower your resting heart rate, improve your fitness, and generally feel better. 
 How we test the best fitness trackers 
 Battery
 During testing we extensively study the battery life of all these devices. Simply wearing them for a few days isn't enough, so we always make sure to run them down completely to get a true feel for how long battery lasts in a given fitness tracker. Obviously your mileage may vary, but we always use them the way most regular people would to give a fair assessment.
 Health tracking and accuracy
 All of our reviewers have extensive experience with fitness and health tracking tech, so we know what to look for when it comes to calorie tracking, heart rates, and sleep. We even test these devices alongside existing tech to look for disparity and erratic results.
 Workouts
 Obviously, we undertake extensive fitness tracking to test the best fitness trackers, conducting a variety of workouts including running and cycling. All of our reviewers engage in a variety of different sports, together they bring years of experience and a huge variety of disciplines to the table.

 Frequently Asked Questions 
 What's the best smartwatch for women?
 We've got a more detailed entry on this topic below , but in short, for the most part there are no major differences between smartwatches for women and men.
 That said, size may be a favor here, so you may prefer to look for a model that's designed for smaller wrists, such as Garmin's Lily range. 
 Some smartwatches also provide features specific to women's health, although in other cases these are options available within the platform you're using and are not restricted to particular models; Apple Watch Series 8 or later, including the Series 11 and Apple Watch Ultra models...
 How do you charge a smartwatch?
 Unlike smartphones, most smartwatches tend to use a proprietary charger, often a magnetic one. Though they are always included with the watch, this can be frustrating if you lose yours or it breaks. 
 Some chargers will work for multiple models – for instance many Garmins and most Apple Watches are capable of using the same charger, although some older chargers may not be as fast as newer ones. Some can also be charged wirelessly either using Wireless PowerShare from a phone or the Qi standard; check your specific model for details. 
 Which model you use, you should generally remove it from the charger once it’s full; though most devices will have built-in safety features to prevent overcharging, leaving your watch on charge for too long could still degrade the device's lithium-ion battery over time.
 How to set the time on a smartwatch
 Unlike with a non-smart watch, setting the time on a smartwatch is simply a matter of syncing the device to your phone via Bluetooth, using the relevant app. The smartwatch will then take the time from the phone.
 What's the best military smartwatch?
 Several of the best rugged smartwatches are also good choices for military use, and you can also buy plenty of non-smart watches from the likes of Casio that have many useful features for the military including top-notch weatherproofing, long battery life, night-vision backlighting and more. 
 Focusing solely on smart models, Garmin offers a range of ‘Tactical Edition’ watches with ‘stealth’ mode, ballistics information (like a compass/golf watch, that takes wind and weapon range into account) and a quick-wipe ‘kill switch’.
 How does a smartwatch measure sleep?
 Smartwatches are a great way to track the duration and quality of your sleep. Whatever the model, a smartwatch will use heart-rate variability information and motion detection to estimate sleep stages and quality – with varying degrees of accuracy.
 Some smartwatches, such as the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 and the latest Apple Watch models, including the Series 11 and Ultra 3, even have advanced features such as sleep apnea detection.
 How do you set up a smartwatch?
 How you set up your smartwatch will depend on which model you have, but all will follow a roughly similar process.
 In almost all cases you'll follow instructions to sync the smartwatch to your phone – either by scanning the watch with your phone’s camera if using an Apple Watch, or by downloading an app – and will then follow instructions from there.
 Every smartwatch will have its own app, whether Garmin, Pixel, Apple, Polar, Amazfit or any others.
 How to choose the best smartwatch for you 
 Unfortunately, your choice of smartwatch often depends on your choice of phone, as not all wearables are compatible with competitor devices. Apple Watch only works with Apple iPhones. Samsung and Google watches, and other Wear OS devices, only work with Android devices, but you can use a Samsung watch with a Google phone and vice versa.
 Dedicated fitness watches from Garmin, Coros and Polar generally offer much longer battery life than Wear OS or Apple watches, often lasting a week or more between charges. If training is your priority, they're worth considering even if they don't offer the same app ecosystem.
 Most wearables will get about a day of battery life, which will be disappointing if you're converting from a Garmin watch that lasts weeks. You can find a few watches that last longer on this list.
 Finally, smartwatches can be expensive, and frankly, they don't offer much value for what you pay. Before you spring for an Apple Watch Ultra, you might ask if you are really going Scuba diving this year, or if you're just going to check your text messages without disturbing your dinner mates.
 The best smartwatch for women vs men: Is there a difference?
 There are no specific differences when it comes to smartwatches for women or men, and choosing the right one usually comes down to personal preference. 
 One of the main considerations is making sure the watch size fits your wrist. Many smartwatches are quite large, which can feel bulky on slimmer wrists, so it’s worth checking the case size before buying. Many models come in multiple sizes, and when that’s the case, we list the options in our full reviews to help you choose the best fit.
 Some smartwatches also include features focused on women's health. These can include menstrual cycle tracking, ovulation predictions, and symptom logging, often powered by data such as heart rate trends, sleep patterns, and skin temperature. These tools can help provide a broader picture of hormonal cycles and overall well-being.
 This doesn't mean those watches are only designed for women, nor that these features must be used. Most are optional and can be enabled or ignored depending on your preferences.
 If you do plan to use them, it's worth checking the privacy policy of the watch you've bought so you understand where your health data is stored and who can access it.
 Can you use Apple Watch with an Android phone?
 The first thing to check is whether your phone is compatible with the smartwatch you want. You can't use an Apple Watch with an Android phone, as all the functions of watchOS require iOS to interface with. 
 You can't use an Apple Watch with an Android phone, as Apple Watch requires an iPhone for setup and everyday use.
 Likewise, Google Pixel Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch models are designed for Android phones and don't support iPhone. If you regularly switch between Android and iOS, a Garmin, Amazfit or CMF smartwatch is usually a better choice because these work with both platforms.
 How we test smartwatches 
 Every smartwatch on this list has been fully and extensively reviewed by the expert team at TechRadar, so we know exactly what makes them tick.
 Our review process involves using the devices as if they were our own personal wearables, ensuring every smartwatch gets fully tested in the real world. A comprehensive sweep of features takes place, and usage is varied over a week to give us a clear idea of how battery life performs.
 When testing in-house, we generally look at how accurate the GPS is on each smartwatch by testing it against an industry leader such as the Garmin Epix Pro . Likewise for workout metrics. We also rank how usable the watch's operating system is, whether it supports third-party apps, and where it sits in the market. For example, a cheap watch with fewer features is more likely to get four stars than a feature-stuffed premium watch that isn't worth the expensive price.
 Using that knowledge we've then ranked them, factoring in their value, design, features, and performance to get an overall star verdict.

 How to choose the best smartwatch for iPhone 
 Choosing the best smartwatch for your iPhone requires you to think about compatibility, features, and your priorities. The first thing to consider is compatibility. The Apple Watch is the best smartwatch for most people with an iPhone. It’s designed to work seamlessly with iOS and it offers great integration with Apple’s ecosystem. Features like notifications, messaging, Apple Pay, and health data syncing all work incredibly well. If you want the most out of your smartwatch, for most people an Apple Watch is the top choice.
 Consider the features you need the most. The Apple Watch offers a range of fitness and health tracking, including heart rate monitoring, ECG, sleep tracking, and blood oxygen levels. Newer models now offer even more advanced features, like body temperature tracking. But if health and fitness aren’t your priority, many of the watches in the guide above offer support for notifications, app interactions, and even cellular connectivity for use without your phone.
 The Apple Watch is considered the gold standard for iPhone users, but other options, like Fitbit or Garmin smartwatches, also work very well with iOS. You may find that they don’t offer the same level of integration but do bring you excellent health tracking features and longer battery life. So if you're primarily looking for a fitness tracker with basic notification functionality, these can be great alternatives.
 A downside of the Apple Watch, at least compared to some other brands, is its battery life. It typically lasts a day or two. This means that if you prioritize longer-lasting battery life over advanced features, you may want to consider alternatives from other brands, like Garmin, which can last longer on a single charge, depending on the model.
 Since you’re going to be wearing it most of the time, the design of the smartwatch for iPhone you choose will be a crucial factor. Apple Watches come in a range of sizes and you can customize them with interchangeable bands, which makes it easy to find a style that suits you. Other smartwatch brands also offer nice-looking and comfortable designs, but depending on your preferences, Apple has the edge in terms of aesthetics and comfort.
 For the best overall experience, especially if you have a lot of other Apple products, an Apple Watch is the clear winner. However, if you’re looking for specific features, like extended battery life or more focused fitness tracking, other brands can still offer a solid experience for your iPhone.
 How we test the best smartwatches for iPhone 
 Our smartwatch process typically involves using the device as if it were our own personal wearable. That's the best way for us to fully test it and see how it fares in the real world. We do a comprehensive sweep of its features, functionalities, performance, battery life, and ease of use, doing so over multiple days.
 Of course, since we also want to know how it performs and which features are available when it's paired with an iPhone, we make sure to squeeze that into our testing as well. Once we've collected all the data and information we need, we take all of it and compare it to the smartwatch's price, finding out if it's a great value for our readers before making a recommendation.
 FAQs 
 What's the best smartwatch for iPhone users?
 The best smartwatch for iPhone users is the one that fits your budget and what you expect it to do; at the time of writing, the Apple Watch Series 11 is our best overall pick for its balance of iPhone integration, display, health tools and everyday usefulness. If you want longer battery life and more structured training tools, the Garmin Venu X1 may suit you better, while the Amazfit Active 2 is our budget option.
 We regularly update this guide as we test and review new watches, so the best overall pick can change. If you are not ready to buy yet, bookmark this page and return when you are comparing current models and prices.
 Should I buy an Apple Watch or a Garmin for my iPhone?
 Buy an Apple Watch if you want a watch that feels like an extension of your iPhone. Setup takes minutes, notifications arrive without fuss, and things such as Apple Pay, calls and apps work in the way you’d expect. For everyday convenience – checking a message on the train, paying for coffee or leaving your phone in your pocket – it’s hard to beat.
 Garmin is the better fit if your watch is primarily a training companion and the thought of another nightly charge makes you groan. The Venu X1 works with iPhone, brings maps, Garmin Coach and Training Readiness, and can last up to nine days with its always-on display off. You sacrifice some of Apple’s polish, but gain the sort of endurance and workout depth keen runners and cyclists will appreciate.
 What is the best budget smartwatch for iPhone users?
 The Amazfit Active 2 is our current best budget smartwatch for iPhone users because it packs in far more than its price suggests. It has a bright AMOLED display, a light, classic-looking design, strong GPS and workout tracking, plus an onboard AI assistant – plenty of useful smartwatch basics, without the usual Apple Watch outlay.
 In our testing, it was comfortable to wear and its calorie and workout figures held their own against an Apple Watch Ultra 2. Amazfit says it can manage five days of heavy use, too, which is a welcome break from daily charging. Want the full watchOS experience and closer iPhone integration? Spend more on the Apple Watch SE 3; the Active 2 is for buyers who want plenty of watch for less.
 Do non-Apple smartwatches work with an iPhone?
 Yes – you are not locked into an Apple Watch just because you own an iPhone. Garmin, Amazfit and Huawei watches can pair through their companion apps, delivering notifications, activity tracking and health or workout data. 
 The catch is that the experience is rarely as joined-up. Third-party watches can be great for fitness and endurance, but app interaction, replying to messages, calls, payments and data syncing may be more limited. Check the companion app supports your iPhone and current iOS version, then make sure the features you actually use are on the list before clicking buy.
 Do Apple Watch health features work in every country?
 No. Apple Watch health features are not a one-size-fits-all deal: availability can vary by country, model, software version and local regulations. ECG, blood oxygen and hypertension notifications are among the features that can differ, so a watch bought in one market may not have exactly the same health toolkit in another.
 If a particular health feature is your reason for buying, check Apple’s current watchOS feature-availability page for your country before handing over your money. And while these tools can be useful for spotting trends or prompting a conversation, they are not a substitute for medical advice – speak to a clinician if you receive an alert or have a concern.

 The final launch of a busy 2026 for Blue Tees has arrived: an affordable, portable launch monitor designed to take your practice sessions to the next level while complementing your existing Blue Tees gear.
 The Rainmaker completes the Blue Tees ecosystem, which already includes the Captain Pro and Captain Air laser rangefinders alongside the Player Pro GPS speaker . Shot data captured by the Rainmaker transfers directly to your rangefinder, dialing in your yardages for each club and delivering tailored on-course club recommendations - more on this shortly.
 Before diving into the wider ecosystem, it is worth looking at the unit on its own merit, as it is a serious new contender for the title of best cheap golf launch monitor . It could even enter the conversation as one of the best budget golf simulators on the market, doubling as an accessible home setup once synced to the companion app.

 So, what do you get for your $600/£600? To start, more than 20 real-time metrics, including carry distance, clubhead speed, ball speed, smash factor, spin rate, and angle of attack. What truly sets the Rainmaker apart from the competition is the built-in LCD display, which shows your numbers directly on the unit without forcing you to consult a phone, tablet, or laptop after every shot.
 All of the metrics tracked on the Rainmaker. 
 (Image credit: Future)
 The device remains genuinely portable and ships with a high-quality carry case. While it technically fits inside an apparel pocket on a golf bag, its weight (719g plus the case) and size mean you probably will not want to haul it around for a full 18 holes.
 Unpack the case and you find a clean unit with an adjustable stand that is simple to set up, complemented by a detachable magnetic remote for menu navigation. The Rainmaker carries an IPX4 water-resistance rating, meaning it easily shrugs off light rain or morning dew, though you will want to pack it away during steady downpours. It also features integrated simulator compatibility, connecting with both E6 Connect and GSPro for indoor play. This is without doubt one of the best portable launch monitors on the market as a result thanks to the versatility on offer.
 The carry case with the Rainmaker is impressive. 
 (Image credit: Future)
 It gets even better if you already use Blue Tees hardware. Having tested both the Captain Pro and Captain Air rangefinders earlier this year, pairing either model with the Rainmaker significantly elevates the experience.
 Get the Golf Monthly Newsletter
 Subscribe to the Golf Monthly newsletter to stay up to date with all the latest tour news, equipment news, reviews, head-to-heads and buyer’s guides from our team of experienced experts.
 Through the Blue Tees app, you create a central hub for your swing data. Every shot hit on the range with the Rainmaker feeds into your profile, mapping precise carry distances for every club in the bag.
 Sync your rangefinder to the app and you can pull this data in real time on the course to receive personalized club recommendations (see our Captain Pro review for a deeper breakdown). The same integration extends to the Player Pro GPS speaker.
 The result is a continuous loop that acts like a digital caddie tailored to your evolving game. Pick up a new driver that carries 15 yards further than your old one? Put in a session with the Rainmaker and your on-course yardages update automatically. Connected ecosystems are increasingly popular across golf tech, with brands like Garmin setting the benchmark, but Blue Tees has carved out a compelling, budget-friendly alternative.
 The kickstand on the Rainmaker makes it very simple to set up. 
 (Image credit: Future)
 As with any entry-level launch monitor, expectations around data accuracy need managing. There is a reason a TrackMan setup runs well into five figures: tracking every parameter with radar-verified accuracy is difficult. Budget units capture a handful of core metrics and calculate the remainder using internal algorithms. If the unit misreads spin rate, secondary calculations, particularly on wedge shots, can drift.
 During testing at the Royal County Down practice grounds, shorter clubs produced occasional outliers. Pitching wedge carries registered up to 10 yards longer than reality on select strikes, though these misreads were fairly infrequent. Through the mid-irons and into the driver, accuracy improved noticeably.
 Testing the Rainmaker at the driving range at Royal County Down. 
 (Image credit: Future)
 Context matters here: Royal County Down's practice range uses standard Callaway range balls. Switching to an indoor net with premium Titleist Pro V1 balls yielded markedly tighter, more consistent figures. As a rule of thumb, feeding the Rainmaker higher-grade golf balls will directly improve the accuracy of its feedback.
 The Rainmaker features three distinct modes: Practice, for standard range work; Speed, for speed-training drills; and Target Distance, which gamifies practice by challenging you to hit exact carry windows.
 While the monitor works as a standalone screen, it truly flexes its muscle once paired with the LAUNCH app. Setting up your virtual bag takes a few minutes - you must log the make, model and loft of each club - but the investment pays off in tracking accuracy. Practice mode renders full 3D ball flights, which proves particularly useful when hitting into a net.
 The LAUNCH app is superb, especially if you are practicing inside and want to see your ballfight. 
 (Image credit: Future)
 The unit also caches up to 1,000 shots internally when running offline, syncing them seamlessly once reconnected to the LAUNCH app for long-term tracking and visualization. While the early Blue Tees app left room for improvement during my Blue Tees rangefinder testing, the LAUNCH platform shows how much Blue Tees can improve its apps in such a short period of time.
 At $600/£600, the Rainmaker delivers exceptional value for money. Keep in mind that unlocking full app utility requires an ongoing $79 annual subscription after the complimentary first year, though this remains noticeably cheaper than competing brands and their subscriptions.
 Ultimately, value hinges on your usage. For golfers logging regular range sessions and pairing the unit with a Blue Tees rangefinder or speaker, joining the wider ecosystem makes a great deal of sense. Even with a few rogue data points on short wedges, the Rainmaker raises the bar for accessible launch monitors, providing a highly capable practice tool for both indoor and outdoor practice.

 This year, I managed to get my hands on two of the best sleep trackers in 2026: the Oura Ring 5 and the Apple Watch.
 While the Apple Watch provides a super-convenient way for iPhone users to understand what goes on while they're asleep, the newly-launched Oura Ring 5, now $399 at Amazon has made headlines for its improved sleep tracking accuracy and sleeker design.
 The Apple Watch 12, now $389.99 at Amazon , is the latest of many Apple Watch iterations, but the good news is that it doesn't matter which model you get if your aim is to track your sleep stages every night.
 So, which popular wearable is the best at sleep tracking: the Oura Ring 5 or the Apple Watch? I've tested both sleep trackers, and here's the one I'm still wearing to bed...
 Oura Ring 5 vs Apple Watch: Price & deals 
 Budget plays a huge role in picking the right sleep tracker, so let's take a look at the prices and deals on both the Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch.

 Let's get one thing out of the way: the Oura Ring 5 is a luxury spend, especially when you consider the additional costs. To begin with, you'll need to buy an Oura Ring Sizing Kit, now $10 at Amazon to find out what size you need to order.
 As for the Oura Ring 5 itself, you're looking at a starting price of $399.99, which creeps up to $499.99 if you want the ring in a Gold or Deep Rose. On top of this, you'll need to pay a monthly membership fee of $5.99, though the first month's subscription is free.

All you need to set up an Apple Watch is an iPhone; this does mean, of course, that the Apple Watch isn't a sleep tracker for those who don't own (or don't plan to own) an iPhone.
 As the Apple Watch comes in different models, there are plenty of Apple Watch deals to suit your budget. As the newest model, the Apple Watch 12, $389.99 at Amazon , will set you back the most, but predecessors like the Apple Watch SE 3, now $239.99 at Amazon , can save you over $100.

 Oura Ring 5 vs Apple Watch: Sleep tracking 
 I've tracked my sleep with both an Apple Watch and an Oura Ring 5 this year (sometimes using them at the same time), and the experience has given me clearer picture of how both perform as sleep trackers.
 First of all, let's explore their similarities. Both take your overnight sleep data and synthesize it into handy, easy-to-read charts and infographics, which you can view on their respective apps as soon as you wake up.
 These charts and graphs explore all the essential sleep metrics: sleep stages ( REM sleep , deep sleep , light sleep ), sleep consistency, overnight heart rate, respiratory rate, and body temperature . And of course, there's your daily sleep score , which summarizes how well you slept with a score out of a 100.

 However, there are key differences. From personal experience, I find it much easier to achieve a high sleep score (often venturing into the 90s) while wearing an Apple Watch than I do when wearing an Oura Ring 5 — and I believe this is a reflection on the depth and accuracy of the Oura Ring's sleep tracking.
 This is because the Oura Ring 5's daily summaries of my sleep are much more comprehensive than the Apple Watch's, as it provides more advanced sleep metrics.
 While the Apple Watch generates its sleep score from three points (interruption, duration, and bedtime), the Oura Ring 5 generates a sleep score from seven: sleep efficiency (time you spent asleep vs time spent in bed awake), restfulness (how many times you moved around or woke up), REM sleep , deep sleep , sleep onset latency (how long it takes you to fall asleep), and timing of your sleep.
 The Oura Ring 5 also provides continuous recovery scoring with its Readiness score, which gives you advice on how much rest you need during the day based on how well you slept the previous night.
 The Oura Ring's Body Clock feature also taps into the new circadian scoring trend , using your sleep data over time to identify your sleep chronotype to show how your sleep routine aligns with your circadian rhythm .
 As for the Apple Watch's sleep-tracking USP, its standout feature is its sleep apnea detection tool (available on the Apple Watch Series 10 and up). It can analyze your breathing patterns and alert you if it detects a high amount of breathing disturbances, which might indicate that you have sleep apnea .
 Oura Ring 5 vs Apple Watch: Design and comfort 
 The Apple Watch has gone through so many eras that it's difficult to summarize its overall design. It's a smart watch, of course, but weight and size can vary depending on the series.
 For example, I wore an Apple Watch Ultra , a model known for its excellent battery life and durability. However, it is a physically large, chunky, and thick smartwatch, which can make it difficult to wear to bed.
 On top of this, I've never been a fan of wearing any kind of watch to bed, so it did take me a while to get used to having this bulky titanium design strapped to my wrist every night. Newer models, such as the Apple Watch 11 , are much sleeker and slimmer, but they can still be pretty noticeable if you don't like wearing wristwatches while asleep.
 (Image credit: Future) Wearing the Oura Ring straight after the Apple Watch was like taking off a pair of uncomfortable boots at the end of a long day. Its sleek smart ring design is completely screen-free, so it looks like an elegant piece of jewelry instead of sleep tech.
 I can barely feel the Oura Ring 5 on my index finger at night (sometimes, I have to feel in the dark to check if I remembered to put it on), and that's probably because its Oura's thinnest, most lightweight smart ring yet (it's 40% smaller than the Oura Ring 4 ).
 Of course, whether its screenless design is a plus or minus depends on your outlook. If you like the fact that you can view your sleep metrics (via the Vitals app ) on your Apple Watch's face without reaching for your iPhone, then you may not like the Oura's screen-free design.
 However, if your priorities are limiting screen time and optimizing sleep comfort, then the Oura Ring 5 is ideal.

 ✅ You want optimal sleep comfort: The Oura Ring 5 has a sleek, lightweight design that provides much more sleep comfort than the relatively bulky Apple Watch.
 ✅ You don't own an iPhone: You need an iPhone to set up your Apple Watch, so consider the Oura Ring 5 if you're an Android user.

 How I built this: based on manufacturer specs and aggregated independent testing — I haven't tested these units personally yet. After writing about how easy it is to get surprised by a $200/year launch monitor subscription, I went looking for the GPS watch equivalent — and the news here is actually good. Unlike launch monitors, where subscriptions are increasingly the norm, the two most-recommended budget GPS watches genuinely have none. No app tier, no annual renewal, no trial that quietly converts.
 My pick
 Garmin Approach S12
 8.3 /10 
 The Garmin Approach S12 is the easiest recommendation here: 42,000+ preloaded courses, up to 30 hours of GPS battery life, and zero subscription — ever. The Bushnell iON Elite is a genuine alternative if you want a bigger, higher-contrast display or slope-adjusted yardages, which the S12 doesn't offer.
 Check Garmin S12 price → 
 Garmin Approach S12
 42,000+ preloaded courses worldwide, updated over wifi/app — no paid course packs
 Up to 30 hours of battery life in GPS mode — several rounds between charges
 Sunlight-readable 1.3" display with a large-number mode for quick reads
 Front/middle/back yardages plus hazard distances; automatic hole advance
 What it doesn't do: no slope adjustment, no shot tracking, no smartwatch features like heart rate or notifications. This is a deliberately stripped-down device, and that's exactly why it stays subscription-free — there's no ongoing service to charge for.
 Bushnell iON Elite
 Larger, higher-contrast display — testers consistently note it's easier to read for users who find the S12 small
 Slope-adjusted yardages built in, a feature the S12 skips entirely
 Automatic course detection and hole advancement
 No subscription for core GPS functionality
 The trade-off versus the S12: slightly fewer preloaded courses (38,000+ vs 42,000+) and a design some testers describe as less refined. If slope-adjusted numbers matter to your game, this tips the decision toward Bushnell.
 Where the no-subscription line gets blurry
 Once you move up to Garmin's higher watches — the S44 or S70 — you're in different territory: shot tracking, virtual caddie recommendations, and full-color mapping. None of these require a subscription for core GPS distances, based on what I found, but they lean much harder on the companion app and connected features than the S12 does. If a watch's headline feature is something that needs live data or software recommendations, that's worth double-checking before you buy — the same way I'd check a launch monitor's subscription terms in my hidden costs breakdown .
 Who should buy which
 Want the simplest possible experience and the longest battery life: Garmin Approach S12
 Want a bigger display and slope-adjusted numbers, and don't mind slightly fewer courses: Bushnell iON Elite
 Want exact pin distances rather than front/middle/back: neither does this — you want a rangefinder, like the Callaway 300 Pro I covered separately
 My take
 GPS watches are the rare corner of this category where the budget option isn't compromised by a subscription trap — both of these are genuinely complete products at their price. If you're deciding between a watch and a rangefinder for exact yardages, that's a different question; for hands-free front/middle/back distances with zero ongoing cost, either of these does the job well.
 Frequently asked questions
 Does the Garmin Approach S12 have a subscription fee?
 No. Core GPS features, including all 42,000+ preloaded courses, work with no ongoing subscription or app tier.
 Bushnell iON Elite vs Garmin Approach S12 — which is more accurate?
 Both are considered accurate for front/middle/back yardages in independent testing. The iON Elite adds slope-adjusted distances, which the S12 doesn't offer.
 Do higher-end Garmin golf watches like the S70 require a subscription?
 Core GPS distance features generally don't require a subscription, but these watches rely more heavily on the companion app and connected features than the S12 — worth checking the current terms for any specific feature you care about before buying.

The question behind this page is narrow and worth being precise about: in this category, almost nothing charges you for basic yardages. What the paid tiers buy is everything around them.
 What a golf GPS subscription actually paywalls
 Here is the distinction that gets lost in forum arguments. Garmin publishes preloaded course maps on the Approach S12, S44 and G12 and does not charge an annual subscription for golf course data — you buy the device and it knows the courses. What sits behind Garmin’s paid tier on its app platform is the extra layer: advanced analytics, certain contest and tournament features, and some cloud statistics history. Shot Scope goes further and includes automatic shot tracking and its performance statistics with no subscription fee at all. Bushnell’s Phantom 2 ships with preloaded courses and no fee for basic distances.
 So the honest version of “no subscription” is: yardages are free everywhere; analytics sometimes are not. If all you want is the number to the middle of the green, every pick on this page gives it to you forever for the purchase price. If you want your round history, strokes-gained style analysis and club averages, read the column in the table below before you buy, because that is where the models genuinely differ.

The honest split: GPS suits golfers who want a number quickly on every shot and play unfamiliar courses; a laser suits golfers who want precision to the pin and have steady hands. In this category the course maps and front/middle/back distances come with the device, and the devices on this page are all preloaded with tens of thousands of courses. Where fees appear is the analytics platform around the device — advanced statistics, history and certain app features — and that is optional. Read what each brand includes before you buy if the stats are the reason you want one.
 Is a golf GPS watch or a rangefinder better? + They solve different problems. A GPS gives you front, middle and back yardages on every shot with no line of sight needed, which is why it suits unfamiliar courses, blind tee shots and fast play. A laser gives you an exact distance to the flag when you can see it, which is more precise. Many golfers who play a lot end up with both. If you are buying one, our rangefinder vs GPS guide is the page that settles it.
 Are golf GPS watches legal in tournaments? + Yes, as long as you use them only to measure distance. Rule 4.3a(1) permits distance and prohibits using a device to measure elevation change, wind or other conditions, or to get a recommended line of play or club. A device may carry those extra functions provided they are not used during the round. None of the devices here measures slope. Check your competition’s local rules too — see are rangefinders legal .
 What is the cheapest golf GPS with no subscription? + At the time of writing, the handheld and clip-on units undercut the watches: the Garmin Approach G12 and the Bushnell Phantom 2 both give you preloaded courses and basic distances with no recurring fee, in a form you clip to a bag or stick to a cart rail. For course management specifically, it removes the guesswork from an unfamiliar hole: you know the carry distance over water before you commit, you know which club actually reaches an uphill green, and you get a breakdown of where your strokes leaked once you are back in the clubhouse.
 Is it worth it?  What separates it from the rest is the analytics layer. Virtual Caddie suggests a club based on your typical distance with that club, factors in wind speed and direction, and shows you where to aim on the map. PlaysLike Distance accounts for uphill and downhill shots. PinPointer tells you which way the flag is when you cannot see it. On a hilly course those three features do more for your score than any amount of post-round statistics.
 The 1.3 inch colour touchscreen is 18 percent larger than the S60 it replaced, sits under a scratch-resistant ceramic bezel, and runs QuickFit interchangeable bands. Hazard View lets you scroll through each hazard on the map rather than tapping through menus. More than 41,000 full-colour CourseView maps come preloaded, which is the deepest mapping in this list.

If you are deciding between an iron and a wedge on an uphill approach, the wind-adjusted Virtual Caddie call removes that deliberation entirely. At 2.08 ounces it is the heaviest watch here, so it is a golf-first watch that you will wear daily rather than a daily-first watch you tolerate on the course.
 It also suits anyone who wants a single device for golf and everything else. Fourteen days of smartwatch battery means you charge it after a round, not every night, and the ceramic bezel takes the knocks that come with a golf bag.
 Where the Approach S62 falls short
 Twenty hours of GPS mode is the trade-off, and it is real. That covers a brisk 18 comfortably but leaves a 36-hole day on a cart tight without a mid-round charge. The simpler S12 runs 30 hours, and if you regularly play long rounds on foot, the S12 is the smarter endurance buy.

 On the course it does the essentials extremely well: front, back and middle green yardages, plus hazard and dogleg distances, with automatic hole progression. Reviewers report yardages within 0-3 yards of cart GPS on most holes, and several international reviews cite sub-2-yard deviation against laser rangefinders. The idea is straightforward: fifteen hours of GPS battery is not enough for a long trip, so you carry the extra capacity in the cart rather than charging overnight.

Quick-release interchangeable bands are included, which is a nicer system than fixed straps.
 Battery life is up to 15 hours in GPS mode and up to 10 days in smartwatch mode. Smart notifications arrive when the watch is paired to a compatible smartphone, and there is estimated activity tracking for steps, sleep and built-in sport profiles. For a golfer who also wants a watch off the course, that dual-mode endurance is the useful part.
 We are including this one with a caveat about the evidence. The rating is 4.0 from 50 ratings, the smallest pool in this roundup, with an 8 percent one-star share. Reviewers generally treat the power pack as a sensible addition that extends play, but they are rating a bundle rather than the watch on its own, which limits what we can conclude about long-term reliability.
 Who the S42 bundle suits
 It suits golfers who play multi-day events, resort trips or 36 holes in a day and do not want to think about charging between nines. The 2200 mAh power pack with both car and wall adapters covers the gap that fifteen hours of GPS mode leaves, and the colour CourseView maps give you the pin and hazard detail the S12 lacks.
 It also suits a buyer who wants colour maps but not the S62 feature set or a membership, and who prefers physical map reading to green-contour data.
 Where the Approach S42 bundle falls short

 Fifteen hours of GPS battery is the second constraint, even with a power bank in the bag. The small 50-rating review pool also means we would not call this the most reliable choice, which is why it sits at the bottom of our ranking despite respectable hardware.  How We Chose the Best Golf GPS Watches
 We scored each watch against the same six criteria, and we weighted them by what actually changes a round rather than by what looks good on a spec sheet. Accuracy came first, then the things golfers complain about most in forum threads: batteries dying between the 13th and 14th hole, subscriptions they did not expect, and touchscreens that misfire with wet hands.
 Accuracy against a laser. The number that matters is not the headline GPS chip but how far the yardage to the middle of the green drifts from a laser rangefinder under trees and near buildings. Reviewers on the Approach S12 report deviation of 0-3 yards against cart GPS on most holes, and international reviews mention sub-2-yard deviation from laser readings.
 Battery measured in rounds, not hours. Hours on a spec sheet mean nothing unless you know how long a round takes you. A walking 18 holes can run four to five hours, and 36 holes can run nine. We translate every runtime into rounds so the comparison is fair. The spread here is large: 10 hours on the TecTecTec ULT-G against 30 hours on the Approach S12, with the S62 and S44 in between at 20 and 15 hours of GPS time respectively.
 Screen readability in direct sun. A transflective MIP panel is dull in a dim clubhouse but superb at noon on an exposed fairway. An AMOLED panel is vivid and colourful but eats battery. Both types appear in this list, and both are legitimate choices for different golfers.
 Course map depth. Yardages to front, centre and back are table stakes. The question is whether you get hazard distances, layup numbers, dogleg carries, hole-by-hole mapping and elevation adjustment on top of that.
 Subscription status. We treat this as a first-class criterion, not a footnote. We noted for every watch whether its core course-management data works with no recurring fee.
 Wearability. Case diameter, weight and band comfort decide whether the watch stays on your wrist at hole 18. We included these numbers in each review because no competitor in this category scores them.
 How a Golf GPS Watch Manages a Round Hole by Hole
 Most roundups jump from a spec list straight to a verdict, which skips the part golfers actually care about. Here is how a golf GPS watch for course management earns its place on your wrist over five hours of walking.
 At the tee box. A good watch finds the satellite and matches you to the course before you reach the tee. On an unfamiliar layout, the front, centre and back numbers tell you whether the green is reachable in two or needs a layup strategy. The S62 goes further with Virtual Caddie, which suggests a club based on your typical distance with that club and factors in wind speed and direction.
 Choosing the layup. Hazard view and dogleg carries are the features that save strokes on holes you have never played. Rather than guessing at a blind corner, you get the carry distance to the corner and the remaining distance to the pin, which turns a coin-flip into a number.
 Managing elevation. This is where PlaysLike Distance earns its keep. A 150-yard flag on an uphill green plays longer than 150, and a downhill shot runs. The S62 and the S44 both adjust for this; the S44 does so with a paid membership, the S62 includes it on the hardware you already own. If your home course has meaningful elevation change, this single feature can be worth more to your scorecard than any stat tracking.
 Blind shots and greens you cannot see. PinPointer on the S62 gives you a direction to the pin when the green is hidden behind trees or a ridge. Green View lets you set the pin manually on a colour map, which is the difference between a guess and a read when the flag is tucked behind a bunker.
 Post-round review. Pair a watch with CT10 or CT1 club trackers and it starts recording which club you hit and how far, then syncs to the phone app for strokes gained analysis and handicap calculation. Reviewers note that auto-tracking can miss a handful of shots per round, so budget a few minutes of manual tidy-up in the car park.
 If you also run or cycle, our guide to the best GPS running watches for marathoners covers the fitness side of multi-sport GPS, but note that a running watch will never replace a golf watch for hole detail.
 Buying Guide: Nine Questions to Ask Before You Buy
 A crowded lineup makes this category harder than it needs to be. Forum threads are full of golfers asking which model in a given range actually fits their play, so these nine questions cut through the noise.
 1. Will you pay a subscription? This is the first filter, not an afterthought. Four of our six picks deliver their full distance data with no recurring fee. The Garmin Approach S44 needs a Garmin Golf membership for enhanced CourseView maps, green contour data, PlaysLike Distance and Touch Targeting. Decide this before you fall for a screen, because a colour display with locked contours is a frustrating combination.
 2. How many rounds between charges? Convert runtime into rounds. Roughly speaking, a four-hour walking round eats 20-25 hours of GPS mode, so 30 hours covers a full week of golf while 10 hours covers two and a half rounds. If you play 36 holes, prioritise the S12 or carry a power bank.
 3. Do you want numbers or maps? Numbers mean front, centre and back yardages plus hazards. Maps mean colour hole layouts, Green View pin positioning and hazard scrolling. The S12 and the ULT-G are numbers devices. The S62, S44 and S42 bundle are map devices.
 4. Do you want elevation adjustment? PlaysLike Distance, which adjusts for uphill and downhill shots, appears on the S62 out of the box and on the S44 with a membership. If your home course has real elevation change, this is the feature that affects your scorecard most.
 5. Watch, handheld, phone app or cart speaker? A watch is the only one of the four that is on your wrist, which means distances without looking in the cart. A handheld has bigger buttons and a bigger screen and never runs out mid-round. A phone app is free and needs no charging discipline if your phone lasts the round. A cart speaker suits groups. If you already have a good phone app and play in a cart, a watch may be redundant. Golfers on forums repeatedly pair a watch with a rangefinder rather than choosing, and that is a sensible middle path.
 6. How big is your wrist? Case size matters more than most spec sheets admit. The S12 is 1.72 x 1.72 x 0.45 inches at 34.1 g, the S44 is 43mm with a 20 mm band, and the S62 is 1.85 x 1.85 x 0.58 inches at 2.08 oz. Check the dimensions against a watch you already wear comfortably before ordering.
 7. Are you adding club sensors? CT10 and CT1 trackers are sold separately and add per-club distance data plus strokes gained. Budget for them as a second purchase rather than assuming they come in the box. Note that auto-tracking can miss a few shots per round, so plan to correct entries afterwards.
 8. Can you use a touchscreen in the rain? Button-operated watches such as the ULT-G work with wet hands and gloves. Capacitive touchscreens need a dry screen and a steady finger. In a wet climate, that is not a trivial consideration.
 9. Is slope data allowed in your competition? Slope-adjusted and elevation-adjusted distances are not universally permitted in formal play. Check your local rules before relying on them in an event, and treat them as a practice and course-management aid.
 Golf GPS Watch Terms Explained
 PlaysLike Distance. A Garmin term for the distance a shot actually plays, adjusted for uphill and downhill terrain, rather than the raw map distance.
 Slope-adjusted distance. The generic name for elevation adjustment across brands. It accounts for the fact that a downhill putt runs and an uphill putt holds.
 Green contours. Coloured lines on a green map showing elevation change, so you can spot where the surface falls away from you. Usually a paid feature.
 Virtual Caddie. A watch feature that suggests which club to hit using your typical distances with each club, adjusted for wind speed and direction.
 Strokes gained. A post-round statistic comparing your performance against a baseline to show where strokes gained and lost. Needs a paired phone app.
 CT10 and CT1 sensors. Garmin club trackers, sold separately, that identify which club you hit and record its distance automatically.
 AMOLED versus MIP. AMOLED is bright, colourful and battery-hungry. Transflective MIP is monochrome, extremely readable in direct sun and far more efficient.
 Hazard view and PinPointer. Hazard view scrolls every hazard on the hole map. PinPointer gives you a direction to the flag on shots where you cannot see the green.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best GPS golf watch without a subscription?
 The TecTecTec ULT-G and the NAVO W1 both give you front, centre and back distances plus hazard yardages with no recurring fee and free lifetime course updates. The TecTecTec ULT-G is the stronger of the two, with 4.3 stars from 5612 ratings, 38,000+ preloaded courses and a 55 g case. The Garmin Approach S12 also avoids a membership for its core yardages, though it is a step up in refinement.
 Is a golf GPS watch worth it?
 Yes, for most regular golfers, because it puts reliable distances and post-round shot data on your wrist without a second device. It is less compelling if you already use a good phone app in a cart. Many golfers use a watch alongside a laser rangefinder rather than instead of one, and find both useful in different situations.
 Which is better for golf, the Garmin S12 or the S44?
 The S12 lasts 30 hours in GPS mode versus 15 on the S44, so it is the better pick for long walking rounds. The S44 has a bright AMOLED colour touchscreen, hazard view, smart notifications and multi-band GNSS, so it wins if you want a watch you wear every day. The S44 also needs a Garmin Golf membership for enhanced maps, green contours and PlaysLike Distance.
 Is a Garmin golf subscription worth it?
 It is worth it only if you use the map features. The membership unlocks enhanced full-colour CourseView maps, green contour data, PlaysLike Distance and Touch Targeting. If you only need front, centre and back yardages, the free tier is enough and you should skip it. Recurring fees are the most common complaint we saw from golfers in this category.
 What is the most accurate GPS for golf?
 Multi-band positioning produces the most reliable lock between holes and on covered holes, and the Garmin Approach S44 uses GLONASS, GPS and Galileo together. For raw yardage accuracy, reviewers report the Approach S12 landing within 0-3 yards of cart GPS on most holes and sub-2 yards from a laser rangefinder. No watch is pin-exact, so confirm anything tight on the course.
 Can I use an Apple Watch for golf?
 A general smartwatch can tell you time, steps and notifications, but it will not give you preloaded course maps, front and back green yardages, hazard distances or PlaysLike Distance. For golf course management you need a golf-specific GPS watch, a handheld unit or a phone app with a golf package. A smartwatch is an addition to those, not a replacement.
 The Verdict: Best Golf GPS Watches for Course Management in 2026
 The Garmin Approach S62 is our pick for the best golf GPS watch for course management in 2026. It is the highest-rated model we found at 4.5 stars from 2109 ratings, and its Virtual Caddie, PlaysLike Distance and PinPointer are the three features that most directly change the decisions you make on an unfamiliar or hilly course.
 The Garmin Approach S12 is the best value, with 30 hours of GPS battery, 42,000+ courses and a 4.4 rating from 3170 ratings, and it needs no membership for its distances. The TecTecTec ULT-G is the pick if you want the lightest, simplest, phone-free watch with no subscription ever, backed by the largest review base in the category. The Garmin Approach S44 wins for everyday wear, and the NAVO W1 and the Approach S42 bundle cover large-screen budget distances and multi-day power respectively.
 Whatever you pick, decide on the subscription question first, translate battery hours into rounds, and hold it against a laser rangefinder on your own course before you trust a tight number. That is the advice we would give a friend buying their first golf GPS watch in 2026.

 The W1 does the simple thing well. You get front, middle and back distances, hazard yardages and score tracking, and more than 42,000 courses load onto the watch with free updates for life. No phone is needed once the course is on board.
 It ships with a magnetic charging cable, a quick start guide and a standard 22mm quick-release strap, so swapping bands is trivial. The two-year warranty is the longest in this roundup.
 Controls are a mix of push button and touch, which suits golfers who want some tactility without giving up a small color screen. The display is described as high-contrast and readable in bright light.
 This is a distance tool and nothing more. There is no course map, no slope reading and no shot analytics, so course management here means picking a club from three numbers.
 Who the W1 suits
 It suits a beginner, a high-handicap golfer or anyone who wants a set of correct yardages at the lowest tier of this list. The standard strap also makes it easy to wear between rounds.
 If your decision-making on the course is front, middle and back numbers, this covers it for a fraction of the cost of the Garmin models.
 Who the W1 does not suit
 With 124 reviews and a 4.1 average, there is far less long-term field history behind it than the watches above. The 10% one-star share reflects buyers who expected premium mapping from a budget device.
 There is also no shot tracking, no virtual caddie and no slope data, so it cannot grow with you the way a Garmin model can.

 It also includes a slope guide, club recommendation, long putt guide, wind direction and a swing speed radar, all without a monthly subscription. More than 40,000 courses come preloaded with customization through the MyVoiceCaddie app.
 Putt View gives green analysis on the putting surface, practice tempo mode works as a training aid, and shot tracking is built in. Battery life is up to 12 hours, roughly 36 holes, with a portable charging dock in the box.
 The 1.3-inch OLED at 390 x 390 stays bright in any light and the touch response works through a golfing glove, which is a genuine advantage in wet conditions.
 What the T11 PRO does that others charge for

 For golfers who read greens more than they read fairway maps, this is the most honest value in the list.
 What the reviews hold back
 The 3.5 average across 115 reviews is the most polarized here, with 44% five-star against 29% one- or two-star. Firmware bricks and charging contact corrosion account for most of the low ratings.

 Affiliate link 
 How to Choose a Golf GPS Watch for Course Management
 Start with the decision you want help with. A golfer who wants to know how far to the pin is served by any watch here. A golfer who wants to know which club is right is served by the S62 and the T11 PRO. A golfer who wants to know why they shot 78 is served by the Shot Scope pair.
 Decide whether you will pay for software. This is the loudest complaint in golf forums we reviewed. Subscription fatigue is real, and it is why five of these eight watches include their core features with no recurring fee. On the Garmin models we tested, full-color CourseView maps, green contours, PlaysLike Distance and Touch Targeting sit behind a Garmin Golf membership. Check that list before you buy, not after.
 Count battery in rounds, not hours. Ten to twelve hours of GPS covers roughly one and a half rounds, which fails a two-round day. The S12 at up to 30 hours and the TecTecTec at about two and a half rounds per charge are the safer picks for travel and multi-round weekends. Forum discussions repeatedly frame battery life in rounds for this reason.
 Match the screen to the conditions. MIP transflective screens on the S12 and TecTecTec are extremely readable in sun and nearly invisible indoors. AMOLED on the S44 and OLED on the T11 PRO look better in both, at the cost of runtime. Touchscreens help with pin placement and maps, but owners consistently say physical buttons beat touch when you are wearing a glove or standing in rain.
 Understand what GPS can and cannot tell you. Front, middle and back yardages are computed from a mapped pin position and your GPS location. A laser rangefinder measures the real distance to the pin where it sits today. Owners comparing both report a 1-3 yard gap, which rarely changes your club but matters on a tight layup. Accuracy also degrades in heavy tree cover and on courses mapped from satellite imagery. Treat the watch as a management tool, not a truth machine.
 Positioning the Garmin models above this list. The S50 and S70 sit above the S12, S44 and S62 in Garmin’s lineup, and neither was part of our eight-watch test group, so we make no measured claims about them. The S62 here is the closest analogue to the upper tier in our data: it carries Virtual Caddie, wind-aware club suggestions, PlaysLike Distance and full-color CourseView maps. If your shortlist includes the S50 or S70, weigh the same four things we measured here: GPS runtime, whether the mapping features you want need a membership, screen readability and case weight.
 Consider the app-dependency trade-off. Golf apps running on Apple Watch or Galaxy Watch give you yardages without a new device, and golfers on r/golf commonly recommend Golfshot and GHIN. The catch is dependency: users report apps going to sleep or losing GPS signal mid-round, and you need your phone charged and paired. A dedicated golf watch works standalone, which is why it is the safer choice for travel and for anyone who plays away from signal.
 If golf is only part of your activity, the broader categories matter too. Our outdoor watch roundup covers general-purpose options, while backcountry GPS watches and hiking GPS watches cover the navigation side of the market.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best GPS golf watch without a subscription?
 The TecTecTec ULT-G is our pick. It gives front, center and back distances plus hazard and shot measurements across 38,000+ preloaded courses, works with no phone on the course, and has no recurring fee. The Shot Scope V5 and X5 and the Voice Caddie T11 PRO are also subscription free, with added mapping or slope features.
 Do golf GPS watches require a subscription?
 Some do, some do not. The TecTecTec ULT-G, NAVO W1, Shot Scope V5, Shot Scope X5 and Voice Caddie T11 PRO include their core features with no monthly fee. On the Garmin Approach S44 and S62 we tested, full-color CourseView maps, green contours, PlaysLike Distance and Touch Targeting are unlocked through a Garmin Golf membership.
 Are golf GPS watches accurate enough for club selection?
 For club selection, yes. Owners of the Garmin Approach S12 report yardages typically within 0-3 yards of cart GPS, and most golfers at that handicap level will not change a club over a one-yard difference. GPS front, middle and back distances are computed from a mapped pin, so a movable pin or a laser reading is more precise on tightly pinned greens.
 Is a golf GPS watch better than a laser rangefinder?
 A watch is better for course management because it maps the entire hole: carries, layups, hazards and doglegs, plus your position and shot history across 18 holes. A rangefinder is better for one number, the exact distance to the pin today. Many golfers carry a watch and add a rangefinder only for approach shots.
 Which is better for course management, the Garmin S50 or S70?
 Neither was in our eight-watch test group, so we did not measure them. The closest model we did test is the Garmin Approach S62, which carries Virtual Caddie, wind-aware club suggestions, PlaysLike Distance and full-color CourseView maps. Compare any upper-tier Garmin on GPS runtime, whether the mapping features need a membership, screen readability and case weight.
 How many rounds can you get from one charge?
 It depends on the watch. The Garmin Approach S12 runs up to 30 hours in GPS mode, and the TecTecTec ULTG covers about two and a half rounds per charge. The Garmin Approach S62 gives up to 20 hours, the S44 about 15 hours, and the Shot Scope and Voice Caddie models sit near 10 to 12 hours, which is closer to one and a half rounds.
 Final Verdict for 2026
 If you want one watch and no recurring bill, the TecTecTec ULT-G is the choice, backed by the largest review base in this group. If you play twice a week and want a Garmin with real battery headroom, the Approach S12 is the better buy.
 Choose the Approach S62 if you want in-round club selection with wind and slope factored in, and the S44 if screen clarity and a slim case matter most to you. The Shot Scope V5 and X5 are for golfers chasing strokes gained rather than better numbers on the tee box, and the Voice Caddie T11 PRO is the pick for slope and green reading without a monthly fee.
 Whichever you land on, check the membership list before checkout and count your rounds against the battery figure. That is how you get the best golf GPS watch for course management in 2026 without paying twice.

 When played at its best, golf is a game built around precision. You only have to watch the world’s best players to see just how accurate they are with their yardages throughout the bag. While distance control is a skill developed through practice and experience, knowing your numbers out on the course can be hugely beneficial for golfers of any ability. That might mean knowing the distance to the pin, working out the carry needed to clear a fairway bunker and much more. Most of us don't have the luxury of a caddie alongside us, which is why GPS devices can be so useful.
 The best golf GPS gear, whether that's one of the best golf rangefinders , the best golf watches or one of the increasingly impressive golf GPS devices, can help you make better-informed decisions that may ultimately lead to lower scores. In recent years these devices have become increasingly sophisticated, but even the more affordable options will generally provide yardages to the front, middle and back of the green.
 With so much choice available though, finding the right device for your game can be a little tricky. Would a watch suit you best? Perhaps you'd prefer a device that allows you to play music alongside its GPS functionality? Fortunately we’ve been testing the best golf GPS equipment and have put together this guide to highlight our favorites across the different GPS categories.

The feature list is extensive but the S70 also handles the basics extremely well, from providing accurate yardages to greens and bunkers to keeping score and tracking shot distances. There are plenty of more advanced features too, including the Smart Caddie tool, which offers club recommendations. PinPointer is another great feature, it's a useful compass that helps you locate the green when faced with a blind shot. You can even integrate weather forecast data into your round, allowing you to factor in the wind.
 It's easy to switch between the regular watch face, which displays details of your most recent round at the bottom, and golf mode when you want to dive deeper into the numbers on the course.  This means testing rangefinders in both bright and dull conditions to assess their performance, using GPS devices across a variety of courses and putting golf watches through their paces both on and off the course. We aim to leave no stone unturned during the testing process, assessing every aspect of a device before reaching our final verdict.
